```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
})

kOutputDir <- file.path("..", "output", "oetjen2018")

ReadOutput <- function(name) {
  path <- file.path(kOutputDir, name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop(
      "The analysis output is missing: ", path, "\n",
      "Run scripts/10_oetjen2018_bone_marrow.R first. ",
      "See the section 'Reproducing this'."
    )
  }
  read.csv(path, check.names = FALSE)
}

OutputImage <- function(name) {
  file.path(kOutputDir, name)
}

verdicts <- ReadOutput("claim_verdicts.csv")
```

## Why this dataset

- Oetjen and colleagues profiled bone marrow from 20 healthy adults by single
  cell RNA sequencing, by mass cytometry and by flow cytometry, and they
  deposited the flow and the mass files in two accessions [1].
- No report in this repository had read a mass cytometry file before this one.
  The two deposits describe the same donors, so they allow a comparison between
  two technologies rather than between two analyses of one technology.
- The cohort spans 24 to 84 years of age, which makes an age trend testable from
  the flow data alone.
- The deposit also ships something the earlier ones did not. It carries the
  depositors' own scatter gate and their own viability gate, in a cytoflow
  workflow file, so the entry into the analysis does not have to be guessed.

```{r}
#| label: coverage

kable(
  ReadOutput("panel_coverage.csv"),
  caption = "The flow deposit. Five stained panels and one unstained control for each sample.",
  col.names = c("Panel", "Files")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: cohort

kable(
  ReadOutput("cohort.csv"),
  caption = "The cohort, read from Table 1 of the paper into gating/oetjen2018_donor_metadata.csv."
)
```

- Two samples are second aspirations from donors who were sampled twice, which is
  why 22 samples come from 20 donors.
- The paper states a median age of 57 years. Table 1 gives a median of 52.5 years
  across the 20 donors and 55.5 years across the 22 samples. Neither reading
  gives 57, and the difference is recorded rather than resolved.

## Part 1: the finding that changes the whole pipeline

- The deposit carries a cytoflow workflow with two polygons. The first is named
  `lymphocytes` and it sits on forward scatter height against side scatter
  height. The second is named `dead_lymphocytes`.
- The second polygon is the important one. It covers the **low** end of the V545
  detector, which is the LIVE/DEAD channel.
- A fixable viability dye normally stains a dead cell brightly, so the usual rule
  keeps the dim events. On this deposit that rule keeps the debris and throws the
  cells away.

```{r}
#| label: gates

gates <- read.csv(file.path("..", "gating", "oetjen2018_manual_gates.csv"),
                  check.names = FALSE)
kable(
  do.call(rbind, lapply(split(gates, gates$gate), function(piece) {
    data.frame(
      Gate = piece$gate[1],
      `X channel` = piece$x_channel[1],
      `Y channel` = piece$y_channel[1],
      Vertices = nrow(piece),
      `X range` = sprintf("%.0f to %.0f", min(piece$x), max(piece$x)),
      `Y range` = sprintf("%.0f to %.0f", min(piece$y), max(piece$y)),
      check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  })),
  caption = "The two polygons the depositors shipped, extracted into gating/oetjen2018_manual_gates.csv.",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

- The `dead_lymphocytes` polygon reaches to about 2,553 on the V545 detector and
  no higher, so a live cell is one that sits above that value.
- This report therefore reads the direction from the deposited gate rather than
  from a convention, which is what `LiveMask()` does.
- The cost of the wrong direction is not an error message. It is a plausible
  looking number. Before this gate was found, the same pipeline reported CD45
  positive cells as 4 percent of live events in a bone marrow sample, and it ran
  to completion every time.

```{r}
#| label: hierarchy

kable(
  ReadOutput("hierarchy.csv"),
  caption = "The median event count at each step, by panel. The scatter gate and the viability gate are the depositors' own.",
  col.names = c("Panel", "Files", "Acquired", "Singlets", "After the scatter gate",
                "Live", "Parent gate")
)
```

## Part 2: resolving thirteen colours across five panels

- Every file came off one LSRFortessa, so the detector names are the same in all
  132 files. A detector names a marker once the panel is known.
- That matters because a large share of the files carry no marker name at all.
  The published panel design is committed as `gating/oetjen2018_panels.csv` and
  it supplies the fallback.

```{r}
#| label: resolution

kable(
  ReadOutput("channel_resolution_summary.csv"),
  caption = "How each channel was matched to a marker across the stained files.",
  col.names = c("Resolved by", "Channels")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: events

kable(
  ReadOutput("event_summary.csv"),
  caption = "The event counts the paper reports, measured on the deposited files."
)
```

- The paper reports a median of 196,000 CD45 positive events collected, with a
  25th to 75th percentile of 100,000 to 278,000.
- The count here is taken before the scatter gate, because the deposited polygon
  is a lymphocyte gate and a count taken after it answers a different question.

## Part 3: whether an automated cut can be trusted here

- The upstream gates now come from the depositors. Everything below them is the
  automated cut rule this repository uses in every other report, which is the
  density minimum with a two component mixture as the fallback.
- The test is simple. Twenty-two samples of the same tissue, stained with the
  same panel on the same instrument, should not give one marker a frequency of 1
  percent in one sample and 99 percent in another.

```{r}
#| label: stability

stability <- ReadOutput("marker_stability.csv")
kable(
  head(stability, 15),
  digits = 1,
  caption = "The fifteen least stable marker and panel pairs, ranked by the spread of the percent positive across the samples.",
  col.names = c("Panel", "Marker", "Samples", "Median percent", "Minimum",
                "Maximum", "Range", "CV")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: stability-verdict

kable(
  ReadOutput("stability_verdict.csv"),
  caption = "The spread of every marker and panel pair in the deposit."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: spread-figure
#| fig-cap: "Every marker of every panel, across the samples. A box that spans the whole axis is a cut the rule could not place."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("marker_spread.png"))
```

- The answer is that it cannot. Most marker and panel pairs span more than 80
  percentage points across samples that should agree closely.
- The consequence is stated rather than worked around. The two claims that need a
  reliable lineage frequency from every panel, which are the order of the major
  populations and which population is largest, are recorded as not measurable by
  this method.
- That is the third dataset in this repository where an automated density cut
  fails, and the cause is different each time. It was rarity in OMIP-043, a
  continuum in OMIP-039 and Yu 2021, and here it is a marker distribution with no
  reliable second mode in a tissue that holds a developmental continuum.

## Part 4: T cell subsets by two technologies

- The T panel and the mass cytometry panel both carry CD3, CD4, CD8, CD45RA and
  CCR7, so both can produce the naive, central memory, effector memory and
  terminally differentiated subsets.
- The mass cytometry route needs different code. There is no scatter and no
  conventional viability dye, so the two iridium DNA channels and the platinum
  channel replace those steps, and the transform is arcsinh with a cofactor of 5.

```{r}
#| label: technology

agreement <- ReadOutput("technology_agreement.csv")
kable(
  agreement,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "The same measure by flow cytometry and by mass cytometry, on the donors that both technologies covered.",
  col.names = c("Measure", "Donors", "Flow median", "Mass median",
                "Spearman rho", "p")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: technology-figure
#| fig-cap: "Each point is one donor. The dashed line is equality."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("flow_against_mass.png"))
```

- The paper reports a strong correlation between the two technologies on the CD4
  and CD8 subsets. This analysis does not find one.
- Two reasons sit behind that, and only one of them is about the technologies.
- The first is the overlap. The mass cytometry deposit covers eight donors, the T
  panel did not gate every flow file, and the donors that survive both routes are
  fewer still. A correlation on that many points has almost no power.
- The second is the CD45RA and CCR7 cuts, which Part 3 shows are the least
  reliable in the panel. A subset built from two unreliable cuts inherits both.

## Part 5: the age trend and the repeated aspiration

```{r}
#| label: age

kable(
  ReadOutput("age_trend.csv"),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "The T cell subsets against donor age, by Spearman correlation on the flow data.",
  col.names = c("Measure", "Samples", "Spearman rho", "p")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: age-figure
#| fig-cap: "Each point is one sample. The line is a linear fit, drawn to show the direction."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("age_trend.png"))
```

- The memory compartment rises with age in both the CD4 and the CD8 lineage, and
  both correlations are significant.
- The terminally differentiated CD8 compartment moves the other way, which is not
  what the literature on ageing usually reports, and this report does not resolve
  it.
- The claim the paper makes is about the memory population, and that claim
  reproduces from the deposited files.

```{r}
#| label: repeats

repeats <- ReadOutput("repeated_aspiration.csv")
kable(
  repeats,
  digits = 1,
  caption = "The two aspirations of the donors who were sampled twice.",
  col.names = c("Donor", "Measure", "First aspiration", "Second aspiration",
                "Absolute difference")
)
```

- The paper reports good concordance between the two aspirations by flow
  cytometry, and the deposited files agree.

## Discussion

### What this shows

- A deposited workflow file is worth more than a deposited panel design. The
  cytoflow file in this accession carries two polygons, and one of them reverses
  an assumption that every conventional pipeline makes.
- The age claim reproduces from the deposited files with a significant
  correlation in both T cell lineages, using an analysis that shares no software
  with the original.
- The concordance between two aspirations of one donor also reproduces.

### What this does not show

- It does not show that the paper is wrong about the correlation between mass
  cytometry and flow cytometry. It shows that this analysis cannot test it, on
  too few shared donors and with the two least reliable cuts in the panel.
- It does not rank the bone marrow populations, because Part 3 measured that the
  automated cut cannot supply a reliable lineage frequency on this deposit.
- It does not touch the single cell RNA sequencing, which is the third technology
  in the paper. Those data are in GEO and not in this archive, so the claim about
  a discrepancy between sequencing and flow cytometry is out of reach here.

### What is left to do

- The authors' full gating strategy is in Supplemental Table 2 of the paper and
  it is not in the deposit in a machine readable form. With it, the lineage
  frequencies would come from stated boundaries rather than from a rule that Part
  3 shows does not work here.
- The unstained control of each sample is in the deposit and this analysis does
  not use it. A cut placed against the unstained control is the obvious next rule
  to try, and it is the one a person uses.

## Reproducing this

```bash
# Pull the two accessions, about 17 GB of the 103 GB archive
./sync.sh pull datasets/flowrepository/FR-FCM-ZYQ9
./sync.sh pull datasets/flowrepository/FR-FCM-ZYQB

# Build the container. Every package version is pinned and asserted at build time.
./containers/build.sh

# The analysis
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  Rscript scripts/10_oetjen2018_bone_marrow.R

# This report
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  quarto render reports/oetjen2018_bone_marrow.qmd
```

- The cohort table is derived from Table 1 of the paper and it is committed as
  `gating/oetjen2018_donor_metadata.csv`.
- The panel design is derived from Supplemental Table 1B and it is committed as
  `gating/oetjen2018_panels.csv`.
- The two polygons are extracted from the deposited cytoflow workflow and they
  are committed as `gating/oetjen2018_manual_gates.csv`.

```{r}
#| label: session-info

sessionInfo()
```
